## Appendix B Proofs for Section 3

We give a brief overview of the CK and NTK here and refer the reader to (Lee et al. 2018; Yang & Salman 2020) for more details.

Consider a model with $\displaystyle L$ layers and widths $\displaystyle\{d_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}$ and an input $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{x}}$. Let $\displaystyle g^{l}({\boldsymbol{x}})$ denote the output of the $\displaystyle l^{\text{th}}$ layer scaled by $\displaystyle d_{l}^{-1/2}$. Suppose we randomly initialize weights from the Gaussian distribution $\displaystyle{\mathcal{N}}(0,1)$. It can be shown that in the infinite width limit when $\displaystyle\min_{l\in[L]}d^{l}\rightarrow\infty$, each element of $\displaystyle g^{l}({\boldsymbol{x}})$ is a Gaussian process (GP) with zero mean and kernel function $\displaystyle K^{l}$. The kernel $\displaystyle K^{L}$ corresponding **[p. 28]** to the last layer of the model is the CK. In other words, it is the kernel induced by the embedding $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{x}}\mapsto g^{L-1}({\boldsymbol{x}})$ when the model is initialized randomly. On the other hand, NTK corresponds to training the entire model instead of just the last layer. Intuitively, when the model parameters $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ stay close to initialization $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{0}$, the residual $\displaystyle g^{L}({\boldsymbol{x}};{\boldsymbol{\theta}})-g^{L}({\boldsymbol{x}};{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{0})$ behaves like a linear model with features given by the gradient at random initialization, $\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}g^{L}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{0})$, and the NTK is the kernel of this linear model. The spectra of these kernels provide insights about the implicit prior of a randomly initialized model as well as the implicit bias of training using gradient descent (Yang & Salman 2020). The closer these spectra are to the spectrum of the target function, the better we can expect training using gradient descent to generalize.

### B.1 Proof of Proposition 3.1

(Hron et al. 2020) show that the self-attention layer with linear attention and $\displaystyle d^{-1/2}$ scaling converges in distribution to $\displaystyle\mathcal{GP}(0,K)$ in the infinite width limit, *i.e.* when the number of heads $\displaystyle d^{H}$ become large. For any layer $\displaystyle l\in[L]$, let $\displaystyle\tilde{K}^{l}$ denote the kernel induced by the intermediate transformation when applying some nonlinearity $\displaystyle\phi$ to the output of the previous layer $\displaystyle l-1$. Let $\displaystyle f^{l}_{\cdot j}:=\{f^{l}_{i,j}({\boldsymbol{x}}):{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\mathcal{X},i\in[T]\}$, where $\displaystyle\mathcal{X}$ denotes the input space of $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{x}}$. They show the following result for NNs with at least one linear attention layer, in the infinite width limit.

##### **Theorem B.1**(Theorem 3 in (Hron et al. 2020))**.**

*Let $\displaystyle l\in[L]$, and $\displaystyle\phi$ be such that $\displaystyle|\phi(x)|\leq c+m|x|$ for some $\displaystyle c,m\in\mathbb{R}^{+}$. Assume $\displaystyle g^{l-1}$ converges in distribution to $\displaystyle g^{l-1}\sim GP(0,K^{l-1})$, such that $\displaystyle g_{\cdot j}^{l-1}$ and $\displaystyle g_{\cdot k}^{l-1}$ are independent for any $\displaystyle j\neq k$. Then as $\displaystyle\min\{d^{l,H},d^{l}\}\rightarrow\infty$, $\displaystyle g^{l}$ converges in distribution to $\displaystyle g^{l}\sim GP(0,K^{l})$ with $\displaystyle g_{\cdot k}^{l}$ and $\displaystyle g_{\cdot\ell}^{l}$ independent for any $\displaystyle k\neq\ell$, and*

$$
K^{l}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}[g^{l}({\boldsymbol{x}})g^{l}({\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime})]=\sum\limits_{i,j=1}^{\tilde{d}}(\tilde{K}^{l}_{ij}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}))^{2}\tilde{K}^{l}_{ab}({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime}).
$$

Similar results are also known for several non-linearities and other layers such as convolutional, dense, average pooling (Lee et al. 2018; de G. Matthews et al. 2018; Garriga-Alonso et al. 2019; Novak et al. 2019; Yang 2021), as well as residual, positional encoding and layer normalization (Hron et al. 2020; Yang 2021).

Consequently, any model composed of these layers, such as a transformer with linear attention, also converges to a Gaussian process. This follows using an induction-based argument. It can easily be shown that the induced kernel takes the form

$$
K({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}})=\Psi\left(\frac{\left\langle{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}\right\rangle}{\left\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\right\|\left\|{\boldsymbol{y}}\right\|},\frac{\left\|{\boldsymbol{x}}\right\|^{2}}{d},\frac{\left\|{\boldsymbol{y}}\right\|^{2}}{d}\right),
$$

for some function $\displaystyle\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$. In addition, since $\displaystyle{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}\in\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}$, they have the same norm, and $\displaystyle\Psi$ can be treated as a univariate function that only depends on $\displaystyle c=d^{-1}\left\langle{\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{y}}\right\rangle$, *i.e.* $\displaystyle\Psi\left(c,1,1\right)=\Psi(c)$.

Using this property and the following result, it follows that the kernel induced by a transformer with linear attention is diagonalized by the Fourier basis $\displaystyle\{\chi_{U}\}_{U\subseteq[d]}$.

##### **Theorem B.2**(Theorem 3.2 in (Yang & Salman 2020))**.**

*On the $\displaystyle d$-dimensional boolean cube $\displaystyle\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}$, for every $\displaystyle U\subseteq[d]$, $\displaystyle\chi_{U}$ is an eigenfunction of $\displaystyle K$ with eigenvalue*

$$
\mu_{|U|}:=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}}\left[x^{U}K({\boldsymbol{x}},\mathbf{1})\right]=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{{\boldsymbol{x}}\sim\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}}\left[x^{U}\Psi\left(d^{-1}\textstyle\sum\limits_{i}x_{i}\right)\right],
$$

*where $\displaystyle\mathbf{1}:=(1,\dots,1)\in\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}$. This definition of $\displaystyle\mu_{|U|}$ does not depend on the choice $\displaystyle S$, only on the cardinality of $\displaystyle S$. These are all of the eigenfunctions of $\displaystyle K$ by dimensionality considerations.*

Further, using the following result, it follows that transformers (with linear attention) exhibit weak spectral simplicity bias.

##### **Theorem B.3**(Theorem 4.1 in (Yang & Salman 2020))**.**

*Let $\displaystyle K$ be the CK or NTK of an MLP on a boolean cube $\displaystyle\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}$. Then the eigenvalues $\displaystyle\mu_{k},k=0,\dots,d$, satisfy*

$$
\mu_{0} \geq\mu_{2}\geq\dots\geq\mu_{2k}\geq\dots, \\
\mu_{1} \geq\mu_{3}\geq\dots\geq\mu_{2k+1}\geq\dots.
$$

**[p. 29]**

### B.2 Proof of Proposition 3.2

First, we introduce the concept of noise stability $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)$, which measures the correlation between the outputs of a function $\displaystyle f$ for $\displaystyle\rho$-correlated pair $\displaystyle(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})$, as $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f):=\underset{(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})_{\rho}}{\mathbb{E}}f(\boldsymbol{x})f(\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})$. Note that $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)$ is related to $\displaystyle R_{\rho}(f)\!:=\!\underset{(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})_{\rho}}{\prob}[f(\boldsymbol{x})\neq f(\boldsymbol{x}^{\prime})]$ as $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)=1-2R_{\rho}(f)$ (O’Donnell 2014).

Using the following result, we can relate noise stability to the Fourier weight of the function $\displaystyle f$ at different degrees $\displaystyle i\in[d]$.

##### **Theorem B.4**(Theorem 2.49 in (O’Donnell 2014))**.**

*For function $\displaystyle f\!:\!\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}\!\rightarrow\!\{\pm 1\}$, the noise stability for $\displaystyle\rho$-correlated pair $\displaystyle({\boldsymbol{x}},{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\prime})$ satisfies $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)\!=\!\sum_{U\subseteq[d]}\rho^{|U|}\hat{f}(U)^{2}\!=\!\sum_{i=0}^{d}\rho^{i}W^{i}[f]$, where $\displaystyle W^{i}[f]\!:=\!\!\sum_{U\subseteq[d],|U|=i}\!\!\hat{f}(U)^{2}$.*

Clearly, $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)\leq 1$ since the minimum degree of $\displaystyle f$ is $\displaystyle 0$. Next, we use the following important result, which upper bounds the degree of $\displaystyle f$ in terms of its maximum sensitivity, $\displaystyle S_{\max}(f)\!:=\!\max_{{\boldsymbol{x}}\in\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}}S(f,{\boldsymbol{x}})$.

##### **Theorem B.5**(Theorem 1.4 in (Huang 2019))**.**

*For function $\displaystyle f\!:\!\text{{\char 28\relax}}^{d}\!\rightarrow\!\{\pm 1\}$, the degree $\displaystyle D(f)$ of the multilinear polynomial which represents $\displaystyle f$ satisfies $\displaystyle D(f)\!\leq\!(S_{\max}(f))^{2}$.*

Using this, and the fact that $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)$ is minimized when the Fourier weight is concentrated on the highest degree term, we get the lower bound $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)\geq\rho^{(S_{\max}(f))^{2}}$, since $\displaystyle\rho<1$ and $\displaystyle S_{\max}(f)\in[1,d]$.

Using the relation between $\displaystyle Q_{\rho}(f)$ and $\displaystyle R_{\rho}(f)$ then finishes the proof.

## Appendix C Related Work

#### Implicit Biases of Gradient Methods.

Several works study the implicit bias of gradient-based methods for linear predictors and MLPs. Pioneering work by Soudry et al. 2018; Ji & Telgarsky 2018 revealed that linear models trained with gradient descent to minimize an exponentially-tailed loss on linearly separable data converge (in direction) to the max-margin classifier. Following this, Nacson et al. 2019; Ji & Telgarsky 2021; Ji et al. 2021 derived fast convergence rates for gradient-based methods in this setting. Recent works show that MLPs trained with gradient flow/descent converge to a KKT point of the corresponding max-margin problem in the parameter space, in both finite (Ji & Telgarsky 2020; Lyu & Li 2020) and infinite width (Chizat & Bach 2020) regimes. Further, Phuong & Lampert 2021; Frei et al. 2022; Kou et al. 2023 have also studied ReLU/Leaky-ReLU networks trained with gradient descent on nearly orthogonal data. Li et al. 2022 show that the training path in over-parameterized models can be interpreted as mirror descent applied to an alternative objective. In regression problems, when minimizing the mean squared error, the bias manifests in the form of rank minimization (Arora et al. 2019; Li et al. 2021). Additionally, the implicit bias of other optimization algorithms, such as stochastic gradient descent and adaptive methods, has also been explored in various studies (Blanc et al. 2020; HaoChen et al. 2021); see the recent survey (Vardi 2022) for a detailed summary.

#### Robustness.

Several research efforts have been made to investigate the robustness of Transformers. Shao et al. 2021 showed that Transformers exhibit greater resistance to adversarial attacks compared to other models. Additionally, Mahmood et al. 2021 highlighted the notably low transferability of adversarial examples between CNNs and ViTs. Subsequent research (Shen et al. 2023; Bhojanapalli et al. 2021; Paul & Chen 2022) expanded this robustness examination to improve transformer-based language models. Shi et al. 2020 introduced the concept of robustness verification in Transformers. Various robust training methods have been suggested to enhance the robustness guarantees of models, often influenced by or stemming from their respective verification techniques. Shi et al. 2021 expedited the certified robust training process through the use of interval-bound propagation. Wang et al. 2021 employed randomized smoothing to train BERT, aiming to maximize its certified robust space. Recent work of Bombari & Mondelli 2024 shows that randomly-initialized attention layers tend to have higher word-level sensitivity than fully connected layers. **[p. 30]** In contrast to our work, they consider word sensitivity, which has been experimentally shown to be similar for transformers and LSTMs (Bhattamishra et al. 2023b).

#### Spurious Correlations.

A common pitfall to the generalization of neural networks is the presence of spurious correlations (Sagawa et al. 2020). For example, Geirhos et al. 2019 observed that trained CNNs are biased towards textures rather than shapes to make predictions for object recognition tasks. Such biases make NNs vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Gururangan et al. 2018 attribute the reliance of NNs on spurious features to confounding factors in data collection while Shah et al. 2020 attribute it to a *simplicity bias*. Several works have studied the underlying causes of simplicity bias (Chiang 2021; Nagarajan et al. 2021; Morwani et al. 2023; Huh et al. 2021; Lyu et al. 2021) and multiple methods have been developed to mitigate this bias and improve generalization (Pezeshki et al. 2020; Kirichenko et al. 2022; Vasudeva et al. 2023; Tiwari & Shenoy 2023).

#### Data Augmentation.

The essence of data augmentation is to impose some notion of regularization. The simplest design of data augmentation dates back to Robbins 1951 where image manipulation, e.g., flip, crop, and rotate, was introduced. Bishop 1995 proved that training with Gaussian noise is equivalent to Tikhonov regularization. We also note this observation is in parallel to our proposition in Section 7 that training with Gaussian noise promotes low sensitivity. Recently, mixup-based augmentation methods have been proposed to improve model robustness by merging two images as well as their labels (Zhang et al. 2018). Several works also use a combination of existing augmentation techniques (Cubuk et al. 2019; Lim et al. 2019). A common belief is that data augmentation can improve model robustness (Rebuffi et al. 2021), and this work bridges the method (augmentation) and the outcome (robustness) with an explanation — simplicity bias towards low sensitivity.

## Appendix D Details of Experimental Settings

We use PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019) as our code framework and as our implementation of LSTMs. PyTorch is licensed under the Modified BSD license.

#### Experimental Settings for Synthetic Data Experiments.

We use standard SGD training with batch size $\displaystyle 100$. We consider $\displaystyle T=50$ and train with $\displaystyle 1000$ samples and test on $\displaystyle 500$ samples generated as per Definition 4.3.

#### Datasets, Model Architectures and Experimental Settings for Vision Tasks.

We consider the following datasets:

*Fashion-MNIST.* Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al. 2017) consists of $\displaystyle 28\times 28$ grayscale images of Zalando’s articles. This is a $\displaystyle 10$-class classification task with $\displaystyle 60k$ training and $\displaystyle 10k$ test images. It is released under the MIT license.

*CIFAR-10.* The CIFAR-10 dataset (Krizhevsky 2009) is a well-known object recognition dataset. It consists of $\displaystyle 32\times 32$ color images in $\displaystyle 10$ classes, with $\displaystyle 6k$ images per class. There are $\displaystyle 50k$ training and $\displaystyle 10k$ test images. It is released under the MIT license.

*SVHN.* Street View House Numbers (SVHN) (Netzer et al. 2011) is a real-world image dataset used as a digit classification benchmark. It contains $\displaystyle 32\times 32$ RGB images of printed digits ($\displaystyle 0$ to $\displaystyle 9$) cropped from Google Street View images of house number plates. There are $\displaystyle 60k$ images in the train set and $\displaystyle 10k$ images in the test set. It is released under the CC BY 4.0 license.

*ImageNet-1k.* The ImageNet-1k dataset (Russakovsky et al. 2015), also known as the ILSVRC (ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge) dataset, is a widely used benchmark dataset in computer vision for tasks such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. There are $\displaystyle 1000$ different classes, and approximately $\displaystyle 1.28$ million training images of size $\displaystyle 224\times 224$. It is released under a non-commercial research use license.

For all the datasets, we use the ViT-small architecture implementation available at https://github.com/lucidrains/vit-pytorch. For the ResNet-18 model used in the experiments on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets, we use the implementation available at https://github.com/kuangliu/pytorch-cifar. Additionally, for the DenseNet-121 model, ConvMixer model and ViT-simple **[p. 31]** model used in the experiments on CIFAR-10, we use the implementations available at https://github.com/huyvnphan/PyTorch_CIFAR10, https://github.com/locuslab/convmixer and https://github.com/lucidrains/vit-pytorch, respectively. All of these models are released under the MIT license.

All the models are trained with SGD using batch size $\displaystyle 50$ for MNIST and $\displaystyle 100$ for the other datasets. We use patch size $\displaystyle 7$ for MNIST and $\displaystyle 4$ for the other datasets. We estimate the expectation over $\displaystyle{\mathcal{P}}$ in Definition 4.1 by replacing every patch with a noisy patch $\displaystyle 5$ times, and sample about $\displaystyle 30\%$ of the training data to evaluate sensitivity.

For the MNIST experiments, we consider a 1-hidden-layer MLP with $\displaystyle 100$ hidden units and LeakyReLU activation. We set depth as $\displaystyle 2$, number of heads as $\displaystyle 1$ and the hidden units in the MLP as $\displaystyle 128$ for the ViT. We train both models with a learning rate of $\displaystyle 0.01$.

For Fashion-MNIST, we set depth as $\displaystyle 2$, number of heads as $\displaystyle 8$ and the hidden units in the MLP as $\displaystyle 256$ for the ViT. We consider a 2-hidden layer MLP with $\displaystyle 512$ and $\displaystyle 128$ hidden units, respectively. The CNN consists of two 2D convolutional layers with $\displaystyle 32$ output channels and kernel size $\displaystyle 3$ followed by a 2D MaxPool layer with both kernel size and stride as $\displaystyle 2$ and two fully connected layers with $\displaystyle 128$ hidden units. We use LeakyReLU activation for the CNN. We use learning rates of $\displaystyle 0.1$ for the MLP with LeakyReLU, $\displaystyle 0.5$ for the MLP with sigmoid, $\displaystyle 0.005$ for the CNN and $\displaystyle 0.1$ for the ViT.

For CIFAR-10, we set depth as $\displaystyle 8$, number of heads as $\displaystyle 32$ and the hidden units in the MLP as $\displaystyle 256$ for the ViT-small model, while these values are set as $\displaystyle 6$, $\displaystyle 16$, and $\displaystyle 512$ for the ViT-simple model. For the ConvMixer model, we use depth $\displaystyle 6$, embedding dimension $\displaystyle 128$ and kernel size $\displaystyle 3$. The learning rate is set as $\displaystyle 0.1$ for ViT-small, $\displaystyle 0.2$ for ViT-simple, $\displaystyle 0.06$ for ConvMixer, $\displaystyle 0.001$ for ResNet-18 and $\displaystyle 0.005$ for DenseNet-121.

For SVHN, most of the settings are the same as the CIFAR-10 experiments, except we set the hidden units in the MLP as $\displaystyle 512$ for the ViT-small model and the learning rate is set as $\displaystyle 0.0015$ for ResNet-18.

For ImageNet-1k, we sample $\displaystyle 20k$ samples from the training set and compare the sensitivity values of pre-trained ConvNext (ConvNextV2-Tiny) and ViT/L-16 with $\displaystyle\sigma^{2}=15$. Both achieved the same training and validation accuracy of $\displaystyle 85\%$, and it ensures our sensitivity comparison is fair.

#### Datasets, Model Architectures and Experimental Settings for Language Tasks.

We consider the following two binary classification datasets, which are relatively easy to learn without pretraining (Kovaleva et al. 2019).

*MRPC.* Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus (MRPC) (Dolan & Brockett 2005) is a corpus that consists of $\displaystyle 5801$ sentence pairs. Each pair is labeled if it is a paraphrase or not by human annotators. It has $\displaystyle 4076$ training examples and $\displaystyle 1725$ validation examples. It is released under the ODC-By or the Microsoft Research license.

*QQP.* Quora Question Pairs (QQP) (Iyer et al. 2017) dataset is a corpus that consists of over $\displaystyle 400k$ question pairs. Each question pair is annotated with a binary value indicating whether the two questions are paraphrases of each other. It has $\displaystyle 364k$ training examples and $\displaystyle 40k$ validation examples. It is released under the CC BY-SA 2.5 license.

For both RoBERTa models and LSTM models, we keep the same number of layers: $\displaystyle 4$ layers. We set number of heads as $\displaystyle 8$ RoBERTa. We use the AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of $\displaystyle 0.0001$ and weight decay of $\displaystyle 0.0001$ for all the tasks. We also use a dropout rate of $\displaystyle 0.1$. We use a batch size of $\displaystyle 32$ for all the experiments. The used RoBERTa model is released on Huggingface https://huggingface.co/FacebookAI/roberta-base with MIT license.

#### Experimental Settings for Section 7.

We set the learning rate as $\displaystyle 0.16$ and $\displaystyle 0.2$ when training the ViT-small with regularization and augmentation, respectively. We use a regularization strength of $\displaystyle 0.25$. The remaining settings are the same as for the other experiments. For computing the sharpness metrics, we approximate the expectation over the Gaussian noise by averaging over $\displaystyle 5$ repeats and set $\displaystyle\sigma$ as $\displaystyle 0.005$.

**[p. 32]**

#### Experimental Settings for Section A.3.

For the experiment with the Adam optimizer, we employ a learning rate scheduler to ensure that the accuracy on the train set is similar to the model trained with SGD. The initial learning rate is $\displaystyle 0.002$ and after every $\displaystyle 8$ epochs, it is scaled by a factor of $\displaystyle 0.5$.

For the remaining experiments in this section, we consider the same settings as for the respective main experiment.

#### Compute Details.

Experiments with synthetic data were run on Google Colab. Experiments on vision and language tasks were run on internal clusters using NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs with 48GB of VRAM. For the experiments on vision data, we use two GPUs and the runtime for each setting is about $\displaystyle 17$ hours. Experiments on language tasks use one GPU and the runtime for each experiment is about $\displaystyle 24$ hours.

## Appendix E Limitations

In our theoretical results, we show that transformers exhibit weak spectral bias, similar to other NN architectures. An important direction for future work is to distinguish transformers from other architectures and show that they exhibit a stronger spectral bias.

Additionally, this work focuses on the inductive bias of the transformer architecture. However, other factors such as the data used while pre-training can also effect the biases these models exhibit on downstream tasks. It would be interesting to explore this effect in the future.

Similarly, the choice of the optimization algorithm used for training can also have an effect. In our experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset (Fig. 11), we see that SGD and Adam are very similar. However, conducting a more thorough comparison, e.g., by considering second-order optimization methods, can be an important direction for future work.
